body_html:
Talking to coworkers in Spanish is a mix of friendly small talk and practical work language. In many Spanish-speaking workplaces, relationships matter as much as tasks: people greet each other warmly, chat over coffee and often have lunch together. Knowing how to ask for help, run a quick meeting or offer to cover for someone will make your working days smoother, and help you build real connections with colleagues.

Key takeaways
  • Greet everyone when you arrive: ¡Buenos días a todos!
  • Most colleagues use tú in Spain; Latin America varies.
  • Ask for help politely: ¿Me echas una mano con esto?
  • Coffee and lunch breaks are key for building relationships.
{{toc}}

Greetings and small talk

  • ¡Buenos días! ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? Good morning! How was your weekend?
  • ¿Cómo va todo? How’s everything going?
  • ¡Por fin es viernes! Finally, it’s Friday!
  • ¿Hacemos una pausa para el café? Shall we take a coffee break?
  • ¡Qué semana más larga! What a long week!

More openers in {{link:small-talk-in-spanish|small talk in Spanish}}.

Talking to coworkers in Spanish: asking for help

SpanishEnglish
¿Tienes un momento?Do you have a minute?
¿Me echas una mano con esto?Can you give me a hand with this?
¿Sabes cómo funciona esto?Do you know how this works?
Perdona que te moleste, pero…Sorry to bother you, but…
¿Me puedes revisar este documento?Can you check this document for me?
Te debo una.I owe you one.

For softer phrasing, see {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

Meetings

  • ¿Empezamos? Shall we start?
  • El objetivo de la reunión es… The aim of the meeting is…
  • ¿Alguna pregunta? Any questions?
  • Perdona que te interrumpa, pero… Sorry to interrupt, but…
  • Estoy de acuerdo con Marta. I agree with Marta.
  • Lo vemos en la próxima reunión. We’ll look at it in the next meeting.

To disagree without friction, see {{link:disagreeing-politely-in-spanish|disagreeing politely in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Deadlines and updates

  • ¿Para cuándo lo necesitas? When do you need it by?
  • Lo tengo listo para el jueves. I’ll have it ready by Thursday.
  • Voy un poco retrasado/a con esto. I’m a bit behind with this.
  • Te mando un correo con los detalles. I’ll send you an email with the details.
  • Ya está hecho. It’s done.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Giving and receiving feedback

Feedback in Spanish-speaking workplaces tends to be warm and relationship-focused. Start positively, then suggest: Me gusta mucho cómo lo has planteado. Quizás podríamos añadir un gráfico aquí (I really like how you’ve approached it. Maybe we could add a chart here). Thank people generously: ¡Gracias, me has salvado la vida! (Thanks, you’ve saved my life!) or Buen trabajo, equipo (Good work, team). When you receive feedback, Tienes razón, lo cambio (You’re right, I’ll change it) shows openness.

Lunch, breaks and after work

  • ¿Comemos juntos hoy? Shall we have lunch together today?
  • ¿Bajamos a tomar algo? Shall we go down for something? (coffee or a snack)
  • Unos cuantos vamos a tomar algo después del trabajo. ¿Te apuntas? A few of us are going for a drink after work. Want to join?

Leaving for the day

  • Bueno, me voy. ¡Hasta mañana! Right, I’m off. See you tomorrow!
  • ¡Buen fin de semana! Have a good weekend!
  • Si necesitas algo, mañana estoy aquí. If you need anything, I’m here tomorrow.

Workplace culture

In Spain, colleagues almost always use tú, even with managers, and the working day may include a long lunch. In Mexico, Colombia and other countries, usted is more common with senior people and clients, and titles like licenciado or ingeniero may be used. Everywhere, personal relationships smooth work: asking about someone’s family, remembering birthdays and joining coffee breaks matter. The Centro Virtual Cervantes offers resources on business Spanish if you want to go deeper. See also {{link:job-interview-in-spanish|job interview in Spanish}}.

A sample conversation

  • A: Oye, Pablo, ¿tienes un momento? (Hey Pablo, do you have a minute?)
  • B: Claro, dime. (Sure, go ahead.)
  • A: No sé cómo sacar este informe del sistema. ¿Me echas una mano? (I don’t know how to get this report out of the system. Can you help me?)
  • B: Sin problema. Mira, haces clic aquí y luego en “Exportar”. (No problem. Look, you click here and then on “Export”.)
  • A: ¡Genial! Gracias, te debo un café. (Great! Thanks, I owe you a coffee.)

Remote work and messaging

With remote and hybrid work, much colleague talk happens in chat apps. Messages are usually friendly and informal: ¡Buenos días, equipo!, ¿Tienen cinco minutos para una llamada rápida? (Do you have five minutes for a quick call?), Te lo paso por aquí (I’ll send it to you here) and Ahora lo miro (I’ll look at it now). Emojis are common, even in professional chats, especially in Spain and Latin America. For calls, see {{link:phone-calls-in-spanish|phone calls in Spanish}}.

And on someone’s last day, a warm goodbye matters: ¡Te vamos a echar mucho de menos! Mucha suerte en tu nueva etapa.

Final thoughts

Greet everyone, join the coffee breaks, ask for help with ¿me echas una mano? and thank people warmly. In Spanish-speaking workplaces, good relationships make good work possible. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted with coworkers in Spanish?
faq.a: In Spain, tú is normal with almost all colleagues. In Latin America, usted is more common with managers, clients and older colleagues.

faq.q: How do you ask a coworker for help in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Tienes un momento?, ¿Me echas una mano con esto? or Perdona que te moleste, pero…
